scope: Orion thermal protection system heritage, Artemis I heat-shield anomaly/root cause, Artemis II mitigation, and Artemis II postflight outcome

evidence_items.claim: The Orion crew module uses a 16.5-foot-diameter ablative heat shield whose outer surface is made from Avcoat bonded to a titanium skeleton and composite skin. NASA describes the Artemis II configuration as using 186 Avcoat blocks.
evidence_items.interpretation: Defines the physical TPS architecture relevant to Artemis II.
limitations: This source describes spacecraft architecture and does not provide an Artemis II measured heat-flux history.
The number of Avcoat blocks is a manufacturing/architecture quantity, not an aerothermal model input by itself.

evidence_items.claim: Avcoat is an ablative material designed to wear away in a controlled manner during entry, carrying heat away from the Orion crew module.
evidence_items.interpretation: Establishes that material loss is an expected part of normal Avcoat operation, while abnormal char liberation must be distinguished from controlled ablation.
limitations: This is a qualitative functional description.
It does not provide a material-response law suitable for predicting Artemis II recession or internal temperature.

evidence_items.claim: Postflight inspection of the Artemis I Orion heat shield identified unexpected char loss across portions of the Avcoat heat shield.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA Identifies Cause of Artemis I Orion Heat Shield Char Loss
evidence_items.interpretation: This is the starting anomaly for the Artemis I to Artemis II TPS decision thread.
limitations: The existence of char loss does not imply failure of the heat shield to protect the spacecraft.
This item alone does not identify the root cause.

evidence_items.claim: NASA determined that gases generated inside the Avcoat during entry could not vent and dissipate adequately in low-permeability material. Internal gas pressure built up, leading to cracking and liberation of charred material.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA Identifies Cause of Artemis I Orion Heat Shield Char Loss

sequence: pyrolysis and ablation generate gases inside the material

evidence_items.interpretation: The anomaly was a coupled material-response and trajectory-environment phenomenon, not simply a single peak-temperature or peak-heat-flux exceedance.
limitations: This evidence does not provide a numerical permeability threshold for use in the MissionLab heating model.
The project must not infer local char loss directly from Sutton-Graves heat flux.

evidence_items.claim: NASA found that during the Artemis I skip-entry profile, heating decreased between atmospheric dips while thermal energy remained within the Avcoat. This condition contributed to gas accumulation inside low-permeability material.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA Identifies Cause of Artemis I Orion Heat Shield Char Loss
evidence_items.interpretation: Time history and internal thermal response matter; the Artemis I phenomenon cannot be represented by peak external heating alone.
limitations: The current MissionLab Sutton-Graves model does not calculate internal Avcoat thermal energy, permeability, pyrolysis-gas pressure, or cracking.
No direct damage model should be derived from this qualitative mechanism.

evidence_items.claim: NASA reported that local areas of Artemis I Avcoat known to be permeable before flight did not exhibit the same cracking or char-loss behavior because gases could adequately vent.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA Identifies Cause of Artemis I Orion Heat Shield Char Loss
evidence_items.interpretation: This observation strongly supported permeability as a key material parameter in the root-cause determination.
limitations: The source does not provide a complete spatial map of permeability versus char loss for public quantitative reconstruction.

evidence_items.claim: The Artemis I heat shield carried pressure sensors, strain gauges, and thermocouples at different depths in the ablative material, providing flight data used to support environmental reconstruction and material-response analysis.
evidence_items.interpretation: NASA's root-cause work used direct heat-shield instrumentation unavailable in the public Artemis II trajectory reconstruction.
limitations: MissionLab does not currently possess these raw Artemis I heat-shield sensor time series.
The existence of instrumentation does not make MissionLab's modeled Artemis II quantities equivalent to measured TPS data.

evidence_items.claim: NASA removed approximately 200 Avcoat samples from the Artemis I heat shield for analysis and inspection.
evidence_items.interpretation: The root-cause determination was supported by extensive postflight material inspection rather than trajectory analysis alone.
limitations: The public source does not expose all sample-level measurements needed for independent material-response reconstruction.

evidence_items.claim: NASA conducted eight postflight thermal test campaigns totaling 121 individual tests while investigating Artemis I heat-shield char loss.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA Identifies Cause of Artemis I Orion Heat Shield Char Loss
evidence_items.interpretation: NASA reproduced and investigated the phenomenon using multiple ground-test methods.
limitations: MissionLab does not reproduce these material tests.
The test count should not be interpreted as a statistical sample for the MissionLab aerothermal model.

evidence_items.claim: NASA reproduced the Artemis I char-loss mechanism in ground testing using reconstructed entry conditions, strengthening confidence in the identified root cause.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA Identifies Cause of Artemis I Orion Heat Shield Char Loss
evidence_items.interpretation: The root cause was experimentally reproduced and was not based only on visual postflight inspection.
limitations: MissionLab does not have the full test matrix or detailed facility boundary conditions.

evidence_items.claim: NASA modified the Artemis II entry trajectory to reduce the duration of conditions associated with the Artemis I heat-shield phenomenon. NASA describes the change as shortening the distance Orion travels between atmospheric entry and splashdown.
evidence_items.interpretation: Artemis II mitigated the known TPS mechanism by changing the entry environment rather than replacing the already-integrated heat shield.
limitations: This source does not provide the exact internal guidance design constraints used to select the final Artemis II trajectory.
MissionLab must not infer that every difference between Artemis I and Artemis II trajectories was driven solely by the heat-shield issue.

evidence_items.claim: NASA technical reporting states that Artemis II flew a modified trajectory without the Artemis I-style skip entry in order to minimize conditions that promoted cracking and char liberation.
evidence_items.source_title: Under Pressure: The Artemis I Heatshield Char Loss Investigation and Artemis II's Successful Entry
evidence_items.interpretation: This provides the clearest public technical linkage between the Artemis I root cause and the Artemis II entry-profile mitigation.
limitations: The abstract does not provide the complete guidance design or all trajectory optimization constraints.

evidence_items.claim: Initial Artemis II postflight inspections found the Orion thermal protection system performed as expected with no unusual conditions identified.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA on Track for Future Missions with Initial Artemis II Assessments
evidence_items.interpretation: This provides an initial postflight outcome for the Artemis II TPS mitigation strategy.
limitations: NASA explicitly described these as initial assessments.
Detailed postflight heat-shield examination and sample analysis continued after this report.

evidence_items.claim: NASA reported that the char-loss behavior observed on Artemis I was significantly reduced on Artemis II in both quantity and size.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA on Track for Future Missions with Initial Artemis II Assessments
evidence_items.interpretation: The Artemis II flight provides initial evidence that the mitigation approach reduced the Artemis I-type phenomenon.
limitations: The source does not provide a public numerical char-loss mass or area comparison.
The word 'significantly' is NASA's qualitative characterization and should not be converted into an invented percentage.

evidence_items.claim: NASA reported that Artemis II heat-shield performance was consistent with arc-jet ground testing performed after Artemis I.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA on Track for Future Missions with Initial Artemis II Assessments
evidence_items.interpretation: This connects the Artemis I root-cause ground-test program to the observed Artemis II postflight outcome.
limitations: The public article does not provide the detailed quantitative comparison between flight and arc-jet test results.

evidence_items.claim: NASA's initial assessment found Artemis II entry-interface velocity was within one mile per hour of prediction.
evidence_items.source_title: NASA on Track for Future Missions with Initial Artemis II Assessments
evidence_items.interpretation: This is useful mission-level evidence that the flown entry state closely matched prediction, but it does not independently validate MissionLab's modeled heating.
limitations: NASA did not state in this article that MissionLab's reconstructed velocity or heating model was the prediction being referenced.
This must not be used as direct validation of the Sutton-Graves model.

evidence_items.mission_context: Artemis III and later Orion heat shields
evidence_items.claim: NASA applied lessons from Artemis I by improving heat-shield manufacturing to produce Avcoat with greater uniformity and consistent permeability for future Orion missions.
evidence_items.interpretation: The long-term corrective action addresses the identified material parameter directly rather than relying only on trajectory mitigation.
limitations: This item describes manufacturing direction, not a public quantitative permeability specification.

decision_thread.title: Artemis I Heat-Shield Char Loss to Artemis II Entry Mitigation

stages.summary: Unexpected char loss was observed on the Artemis I Orion heat shield after flight.
NASA combined flight instrumentation, postflight sampling, nondestructive evaluation, modeling, and extensive ground testing.
Low-permeability Avcoat restricted pyrolysis-gas venting during the skip-entry thermal history, allowing internal pressure to build and produce cracking and char liberation.
The already-manufactured Artemis II heat shield had to be flown with a safe entry environment supported by the investigation and test evidence.
NASA modified the Artemis II entry trajectory, reducing exposure to conditions associated with the Artemis I phenomenon and avoiding the Artemis I-style skip entry.
Initial postflight inspections found Artemis II TPS performance as expected, with Artemis I-type char loss substantially reduced.
Future Orion heat-shield manufacturing incorporates improvements intended to produce more uniform and consistently permeable Avcoat.

relationship_to_phase2e4_heating_model: Phase 2E.4 reconstructs a low-fidelity external stagnation-point convective-heating environment.
Phase 2F evidence describes Orion material behavior, investigation findings, operational mitigation, and postflight outcomes.
The Sutton-Graves heat-flux history must not be converted directly into Avcoat crack probability, char-loss amount, recession depth, bondline temperature, or crew risk.
The Artemis I root cause depended on material permeability, internal gas pressure, and thermal time history, quantities not modeled by Phase 2E.4.
Artemis II postflight TPS observations provide heritage and outcome context but are not a direct numerical validation of MissionLab's Sutton-Graves heat flux.
allowed_uses: construct an evidence-grounded TPS decision thread
provide heritage context beside the modeled Artemis II entry environment
compare mission timeline and qualitative entry-profile structure
distinguish expected controlled ablation from anomalous char liberation
document how Artemis I findings affected Artemis II operations and future heat-shield manufacturing
prohibited_inferences: predict Artemis II char-loss quantity from Sutton-Graves heat flux alone
predict Avcoat recession depth without a material-response model
predict internal heat-shield temperature without TPS thermal-response data
treat Artemis II reduced char loss as numerical validation of the MissionLab heating model
invent quantitative permeability limits not published by NASA
calibrate the Sutton-Graves model to Artemis I or Artemis II char-loss observations
